This is a 48-year-old male who attends the emergency department with a four-day history of continuous abdominal pain localized to the right lower quadrant. The pain was accompanied by two episodes of diarrhea, and the patient also reported having a fever on two occasions, with temperatures exceeding 38°C. The patient stated that he received treatment from a general practitioner with butyl hyoscine and metoclopramide, which did not improve his condition. Upon admission, a physical examination was performed with the following findings: scar from a previous appendectomy, absence of bowel sounds, abdominal distension with positive rebound tenderness, positive McBurney's sign, positive Psoas sign, positive Obturator sign, as well as signs of peritoneal irritation (involuntary rigidity of the abdomen, pain to fine, superficial touch).

fields.subject: index_patient
fields.name: Infraumbilical incision and layered dissection into right abdominal cavity
fields.body_site: infraumbilical abdomen and right abdominal cavity

evidence.quote: infraumbilical incision was made, with dissection through the layers until entering the right abdominal cavity

facts.clinical_statement: Infraumbilical incision and layered dissection into right abdominal cavity

evidence.quote: edematous and erythematous appendiceal stump

Based on the clinical presentation of acute abdomen, imaging findings, and his prior history of appendectomy, an alternative etiology was initially suspected, prompting an open surgical approach. Regarding the surgical procedure performed: An infraumbilical incision was made, with dissection through the layers until entering the right abdominal cavity, where an edematous and erythematous appendiceal stump was found, confirming the diagnosis of stump appendicitis (Figure 2A). The stump was ligated at its base, the inflammatory phlegmon was dissected, and stump appendectomy was performed (Figure 2B) using the Halstead technique. The abdominal cavity was then irrigated, followed by layered closure, and the procedure was concluded. Diagnostic laparoscopy was not performed, as the necessary equipment was unavailable at our hospital. If stump appendicitis had been considered from the outset and laparoscopic access had been possible, a laparoscopic appendectomy would have been the preferred approach, offering faster recovery and lower morbidity and mortality.

summary.text: A 48-year-old man described as from Chihuahua, Mexico, with appendectomy several years earlier, presented with four days of continuous right-lower-quadrant pain, two diarrhea episodes and two fevers above 38 °C. GP butyl hyoscine/metoclopramide did not help. Examination showed an appendectomy scar, absent bowel sounds, distension, rebound/McBurney/psoas/obturator signs, involuntary rigidity and superficial-touch pain. WBC was printed as 14.55 cells/mm³ with reference 4.5–10.5; neutrophils 8.93 cells/mm³ were described without neutrophilia, with no inferred multiplier. Oral-contrast CT showed pericecal fat inflammation and phlegmon; constipation, gastroenteritis and right-sided diverticulitis were considered then refuted. Open emergency exploration through an infraumbilical incision confirmed an edematous erythematous appendiceal stump. Base ligation, phlegmon dissection and Halstead completion appendectomy were followed by irrigation/layered closure. Diagnostic laparoscopy was unavailable because of missing equipment. A caption AI-estimated stump length 0.67 cm requires review. Good postoperative progress the following day prompted indicated home discharge with unspecified analgesic/antibiotic treatment; actual discharge completion is not explicit. Histopathology obtained weeks later showed acute fibrinopurulent appendicitis, purulent peritonitis and a 4×4 cm phlegmon. At a consultation reported one month later he continued to improve and was discharged from surgical care.

evidence.quote: It is a rare and underestimated entity, especially when classic clinical symptoms are present but there is a history of appendectomy; it leads to initial differential diagnoses, delaying treatment and leading to fatal complications. Here, we present the case of an adult male with right lower quadrant pain, fever, and a history of appendectomy. Stump appendicitis was diagnosed via computed tomography (CT), and the patient underwent emergency exploratory laparotomy.

Based on the clinical presentation of acute abdomen, imaging findings, and his prior history of appendectomy, an alternative etiology was initially suspected, prompting an open surgical approach. Regarding the surgical procedure performed: An infraumbilical incision was made, with dissection through the layers until entering the right abdominal cavity, where an edematous and erythematous appendiceal stump was found, confirming the diagnosis of stump appendicitis (Figure 2A). The stump was ligated at its base, the inflammatory phlegmon was dissected, and stump appendectomy was performed (Figure 2B) using the Halstead technique. The abdominal cavity was then irrigated, followed by layered closure, and the procedure was concluded. Diagnostic laparoscopy was not performed, as the necessary equipment was unavailable at our hospital. If stump appendicitis had been considered from the outset and laparoscopic access had been possible, a laparoscopic appendectomy would have been the preferred approach, offering faster recovery and lower morbidity and mortality.
